answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a Cosmos/DocumentDB account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2 --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: use resource type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' (e.g. resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... }). Terraform (azurerm provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) connection string: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@  (mongodb+srv://<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com is also supported in regions that expose SRV). Port: 10255 for TLS. Required options usually include ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb and often retryWrites=false.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB is billed by Request Units (RUs) when using provisioned throughput (manual or autoscale). There is also a serverless mode in supported regions for low-throughput workloads. The primary capacity model is RU/s (not vCores).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: MongoDB API on Cosmos DB traditionally uses username/password credentials derived from the account keys (SCRAM-style auth via the MongoDB driver). Microsoft Entra ID (AAD) token authentication for the MongoDB API is not generally available (AAD is available for Cosmos DB SQL API management/data-plane in newer releases, but for MongoDB API you normally authenticate with the account user/password in the connection string).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g. npm package 'mongodb' for Node.js). For management/ARM tasks use the Azure Cosmos (Microsoft.DocumentDB) management SDK/az CLI, but for data-plane queries and CRUD with the MongoDB API you use the vanilla MongoDB client.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: When vector-capable Cosmos DB clusters are enabled, vector indexes are created via the MongoDB createIndex command on the vector field. Example (mongo shell / Node driver): db.carts.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', engine: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dims: 1536 })  — (note: exact option names vary by provider; use createIndex on the vector field with engine/algorithm options such as hnsw, ivf or diskann as supported by the cluster).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB does not expose the MongoDB Atlas 'Atlas Search' engine; for lexical/full-text search you typically integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search (indexing documents into Search) or use a separate search service. Hybrid relevance+vector workflows are implemented by combining Cosmos DB vector search (if available) with Azure Cognitive Search or an application-level combination step.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supports a subset of MongoDB server versions / wire protocols (you choose the 'server version' at account creation — historically 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4/5.0 and later additions up to 6.x in newer accounts). Some MongoDB features are limited or unsupported: certain server-side JavaScript/mapReduce operations, some aggregation pipeline stages or admin commands, and cross-partition multi-document transactions historically have limited behavior. Expect gaps vs. a native MongoDB server and verify the exact supported server version on the account.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: For MongoDB-compatible development, run a standard MongoDB docker image (e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo mongo:6.0) and connect on port 27017. The Azure Cosmos DB emulator exists for the SQL API and some APIs, but it may not fully support the MongoDB API feature set; for full MongoDB protocol compatibility use a local MongoDB server image.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB provides a Change Feed feature (Cosmos change feed) which must be used via the Cosmos SDK / Functions / Change Feed Processor; MongoDB change streams are not generally available in the same way on Cosmos MongoDB API accounts. So you should use Cosmos DB Change Feed (enable/consume it) for change notifications rather than relying on MongoDB change streams.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (service-specific) for data-plane inspection and tools; the general azure MCP server covers ARM/management-plane interactions but not the service-specific data-plane helpers for DocumentDB/Mongo API.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's proprietary document database service which was rebranded under the umbrella Azure Cosmos DB. The 'DocumentDB' name historically refers to Microsoft's service; this is separate from any open-source 'DocumentDB' projects. The MongoDB API is a compatibility layer on top of Cosmos DB's engine.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is Microsoft's Cosmos DB proprietary engine providing MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility. Application code uses standard MongoDB drivers, but you must avoid MongoDB server features not implemented by Cosmos (verify aggregation stages, transactions semantics, admin commands). Also tune connection options (ssl/tls, replicaSet=globaldb) and throughput (RUs).

answers.question: What database name should this sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named 'sample_retail_12' for all sample data and collections.

answers.question: How will the sample read the cluster endpoint and what format is expected in DOCUMENTDB_URI?
answers.answer: Read the full MongoDB connection string from environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. Expect a mongodb:// or mongodb+srv:// URI that already includes username and password (or use a placeholder and supply credentials via environment). Example expected format: mongodb://<user>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false

answers.question: Which collections and indexes will the sample create for the abandoned-cart pipeline?
answers.answer: Create a 'carts' collection in database 'sample_retail_12' partitioned by customerId. Create a TTL or timestamp index on lastUpdated for querying abandoned carts and a vector index on the embedding field for similarity: Example mongo commands: db.createCollection('carts', {validator:{}, shardKey:{customerId:1}}) ; db.carts.createIndex({ lastUpdated: 1 }); db.carts.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', engine: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', dims: 1536 })

answers.question: Which Node.js client and connection code will the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the official mongodb Node.js driver (npm install mongodb). Connect with: const client = new MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { tls: true, useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }); await client.connect(); then use client.db('sample_retail_12').collection('carts').

answers.question: How should the sample log outcomes back to DocumentDB?
answers.answer: Use upsert/updateOne to record send status on the cart document, e.g. db.carts.updateOne({ cartId: '...' }, { $set: { recoverySent: true, channel: 'email', sentAt: new Date(), outcome: 'delivered' } }, { upsert: false }). If you need atomicity across multiple docs, use a transaction only if the account's MongoDB API version supports the required transaction semantics.
